extracted.intended_audience: practitioners admitted to practice before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), OED attorneys, and tribunals handling USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO Tribunal / OED to determine whether a practitioner violated the Rules of Professional Conduct and to select appropriate disciplinary sanctions, including enumerated rules, required recordkeeping, burden/standard of proof, and aggravating/mitigating factors (ABA Standards) governing penalty determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) — duty to cooperate in investigations / respond to lawful demand
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner, in connection with a disciplinary matter, shall not fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely, fully, and directly respond to OED RFIs and Lack of Cooperation letters constitutes non-cooperation. Good faith effort and timeliness are required; unexplained delays or persistent failure to respond are not excusable. Repeated or continued failure to produce requested records during investigation supports a finding under §11.801(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice is broader than merely failing to follow formal rules; it includes not abiding by court-established rules (including their spirit). Failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigations or otherwise obstructing processes can qualify as prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a) — separate account and five-year record retention
rubrics_metrics.description: [A client's f]unds shall be kept in a separate account maintained in the state where the practitioner's office is situated ... Complete records of such account funds and other property shall be kept by the practitioner and shall be preserved for a period of five years after termination of the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must maintain 'complete records' of IOLTA/trust accounts for five years after representation ends. Partial or fragmentary records (e.g., only deposit slips or a single monthly statement) do not satisfy the 'complete records' requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(i) — receipt and disbursement journals requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include receipt and disbursement journals containing a record of deposits to and withdrawals from client trust accounts, specifically identifying the date, source, and description of each item deposited, as well as the date, payee and purpose of each disbursement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'journal' is a book of original entry; entries must clearly identify date, source, description of deposits and date/payee/purpose of disbursements. Absence of such journals supports a finding of inadequate recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(ii) — ledger records requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include ledger records for all client trust accounts showing, for each separate trust client or beneficiary, the source of all funds deposited, the names of all persons for whom the funds are or were held, the amount of such funds, the descriptions and amounts of charges or withdrawals, and the names of all persons or entities to whom such funds were disbursed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'ledger' is a book containing accounts to which debits and credits are posted from books of original entry. Ledgers must permit reconstruction of individual client balances and transactions. Producing an invoice alone is not necessarily a sufficient ledger.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(iv) — copies of accountings to clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include copies of accountings to clients or third persons showing the disbursement of funds to them or on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountings provided to clients should be retained as part of the trust-account records. Lack of retained accountings undermines compliance with recordkeeping obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(vi) — copies of records showing disbursements
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include copies of records showing disbursements on behalf of clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must retain documentary evidence of disbursements (checks, cashier's checks, payment copies). Failure to retain these records supports finding of incomplete trust-account records.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(vii) — equivalents of checkbook registers, bank statements, cancelled checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include the physical or electronic equivalents of all checkbook registers, bank statements, records of deposit, pre-numbered canceled checks, and substitute checks provided by a financial institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monthly bank statements and canceled checks (or electronic equivalents) are essential; isolated deposit slips or cashier's checks are inadequate substitutes for complete monthly account statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(viii) — records of electronic transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include records of all electronic transfers from client trust accounts, including the name of the person authorizing transfer, the date of transfer, the name of the recipient and confirmation from the financial institution of the trust account number from which money was withdrawn and the date and the time the transfer was completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed electronic-transfer records (authorization, recipient, timestamps, confirmation) must be retained for trust-account compliance; absence is a recordkeeping violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1)(ix) — monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records include copies of monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations of the client trust accounts maintained by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must perform and retain reconciliations and trial balances regularly; failure to keep them undermines the ability to verify trust-account integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(c) — deposit of advance payments into trust until earned
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawyer shall deposit into a client trust account legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance, to be withdrawn by the lawyer only as fees are earned or expenses incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance/flat fee payments must be held in trust until earned. A lawyer does not earn flat fees upon receipt; fees are earned by conferring a benefit or performing services. Withdrawing advance payments before they are earned violates the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof — clear and convincing evidence for findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings of violation in disciplinary proceedings are established by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal applied the clear and convincing standard to find violations of the Rules of Professional Conduct based on record evidence (e.g., missing records, failures to respond).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2) — authorized sanctions and authority to impose conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a finding of violation, the Tribunal is authorized to impose an order of suspension, exclusion, reprimand and/or probation and also may impose any conditions deemed appropriate under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions may be combined and tailored (e.g., stay of suspension with probation and specific conditions such as restitution, testing, treatment). The Tribunal's authority includes conditioning reinstatement on restitution, professional responsibility courses, or other appropriate conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factor (1) — violation of duty owed (to client/public/system/profession)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sanction, consider whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiduciary breaches (diligence failures, misrepresentations, poor communication) weigh heavily. The Tribunal evaluates the nature of the duty breached and the betrayal of client/professional trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factor (2) — practitioner's mental state (intentional/knowing/negligent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional or knowing misconduct often warrants greater discipline than negligent conduct. 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question; knowledge may be inferred from circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factor (3) — amount of actual or potential injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both actual financial loss and potential harms (e.g., loss of patent rights under first-inventor-to-file rules) are relevant. Lack of proven actual harm does not preclude finding misconduct or applying discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factor (4) — existence of aggravating or mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors in determining the appropriate sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating and mitigating factors (per ABA Standards) are analyzed in context; their presence or absence can increase or reduce discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: prior disciplinary offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior disciplinary offenses may justify an increase in discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal prior discipline is a strong aggravator; contemporaneous warning letters or prior misconduct patterns also inform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: dishonest or selfish motive
rubrics_metrics.description: A dishonest or selfish motive is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions motivated by personal gain or deceit (e.g., misrepresenting work status to conceal neglect) increase severity of sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: pattern of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of misconduct is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated similar misconduct (e.g., recurring failures to communicate or meet deadlines) supports harsher sanctions even absent prior formal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: multiple offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple offenses are an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct instances of misconduct across counts or clients increase culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: bad faith obstruction of disciplinary proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally ignoring RFIs, failing to produce documents, or submitting false statements during proceedings qualifies as obstruction and aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: submission of false evidence or deceptive practices in proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission of false evidence, false statements, or other deceptive practices during the disciplinary process is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentations to investigative bodies (e.g., Washington State Bar) or to the Tribunal are significant aggravators.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to acknowledge the wrongful nature of conduct is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of remorse, refusal to admit fault, or failure to rectify harms weigh against mitigation and support stricter sanctions (e.g., MPRE requirement, probation).

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: vulnerability of victim
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulnerability of the victim is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the client or third party was particularly vulnerable, this increases seriousness of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: substantial experience in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial experience in the practice of law is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced practitioners are expected to understand and follow ethical rules; extensive experience can increase culpability where misconduct occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: indifference to making restitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Indifference to making restitution is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure or refusal to repay clients for losses or return unearned fees increases severity of sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — aggravating: illegal conduct (including controlled substances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illegal conduct, including that involving the use of controlled substances, is an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal conduct related to professional practice significantly aggravates discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: absence of a prior disciplinary record
rubrics_metrics.description: An absence of a prior disciplinary record is a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of prior formal discipline may reduce the degree of sanction when present and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: absence of a dishonest or selfish motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of a dishonest or selfish motive is a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where misconduct appears non-purposeful or not motivated by selfish gain, mitigation may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: personal or emotional problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal or emotional problems may be a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented personal/emotional issues that contributed to misconduct can mitigate, subject to verification and appropriate conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: timely good faith effort to make restitution or rectify consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely good faith effort to make restitution or to rectify consequences of misconduct is mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt restitution or corrective measures can substantially reduce recommended discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: full and free disclosure and cooperative attitude toward proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Full and free disclosure to the disciplinary board or cooperative attitude toward proceedings is mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation with investigators and truthful engagement with the process weighs in favor of mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: inexperience in the practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Inexperience in the practice of law may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newer practitioners may receive some mitigation for mistakes stemming from lack of experience, though not for dishonest conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: character or reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of good character or reputation may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong character references and community standing can be considered in mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: physical disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical disability may be a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented physical impairments linked to misconduct can mitigate if adequately demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: mental disability or chemical dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental disability or chemical dependency may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verified mental-health or substance-abuse issues that contributed to misconduct can mitigate and support rehabilitation conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: delay in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in disciplinary proceedings may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay by the disciplinary system can be a mitigating consideration in determining sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: imposition of other penalties or sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of other penalties or sanctions may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the practitioner has already been sanctioned elsewhere for the same misconduct, that may reduce additional sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: Remorse is a mitigating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine remorse accompanied by corrective action supports mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards — mitigating: remoteness of prior offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Remoteness of prior offenses may be mitigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old misdeeds far in the past that are not recent may be afforded less weight as aggravation.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards Rule 9.4 — factors not to be considered in mitigation/aggravation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain factors should not be considered either as aggravating or mitigating: forced or compelled restitution; agreeing to a client's demand for certain improper behavior or result; withdrawal of complaint against the lawyer; resignation prior to completion of disciplinary proceedings; complainant's recommendation as to sanction; failure of injured client to complain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunals should avoid reliance on these factors when calibrating discipline per ABA guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of discipline — protection of public and deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of attorney discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice; deterrence of others is an important function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions prioritize public protection over punishment; deterrent effect and maintenance of public confidence in the profession are relevant to sanction selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.1 — definition of 'knowingly'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question. A person's knowledge may be inferred from circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental-state assessments in discipline hinge on this definition; circumstantial evidence may support an inference of actual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping definitions — journal and ledger defined
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Journal' is a book of original entry in double-entry bookkeeping; 'ledger' is a book containing accounts to which debits and credits resulting from business transactions are posted from books of original entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding these accounting terms is necessary to assess adequacy of trust-account records; absence of these conventional records is probative of noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No double-counting / duplicate liability for same conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent should not be found liable under multiple counts for the same conduct where one finding already addresses that conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal may decline to find additional violations under identical rule provisions if the conduct has already been adjudicated under the same rule and facts (avoid duplicative findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible conditions of probation or reinstatement (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probation may be imposed in lieu of or in addition to other sanctions; conditions may include restitution, successful completion of a professional responsibility course or examination, neuropsychological assessment, or other treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions must be stated in the order imposing probation and may include client-notification duties; these represent typical remedial/rehabilitative measures the Tribunal may require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness to practice — ultimate disciplinary inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate issue in disciplinary proceedings is whether the respondent is fit to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal evaluates misconduct, mitigation/aggravation, remediation, and fitness for future practice when imposing discipline, up to disbarment/exclusion.
